paragraphs.text: St. Paul presents himself as an apostle of Christ, and states that this apostleship came about according to the will of God. He sends his greetings, and those of his disciple Timothy, to the people of Colossae.
He greets the believers (the saints), granting them the apostolic blessing and asking for them grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

So that your life and your works may be according to the will of God, you need prayer before everything else, and you need to be ready to accept God's adverse dispositions, confident that they are for your good. Then God will always reveal His will to you, and will correct your course if you stray from it through not knowing, so that you walk in assurance, confident of your words and your actions, which are upheld by the power of God.

entries.section: (2) Praise for their faith and love

paragraphs.text: "We give thanks ... always": that we may learn from this to give thanks to God in all our prayers for all the matters of our lives.

"God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ": the "and" here does not mean two separate persons, but two hypostatic attributes of one God, the attribute of Fatherhood and the attribute of Sonship. It is as when we say, "So-and-so is a physician and a literary athlete": we do not mean three persons, but one person with three attributes.
The Apostle always gives thanks to God, and so most of his epistles begin with thanksgiving, just as our Church takes care in all her liturgical prayers to begin them with the prayer of thanksgiving.

St. Paul is an ideal servant, for he prays for people he had never seen in his life. Do we pray for our loved ones and our brethren in the faith, and indeed for all people, whether in our own country or in the whole world, especially when we hear of disasters, famines or disturbances, confident that our prayer has great value before our loving God?

entries.section: (2) Praise for their faith and love

paragraphs.text: The Apostle tells them that his thanksgiving to God was for what he had heard about them of a practical faith, one that works through love.
So, my brethren, let us not be content with a theoretical faith, for that is a faith like that of the demons, but let us prove our faith by works of love.

entries.section: (2) Praise for their faith and love

paragraphs.text: When the proclamation of the Gospel reached the people of Colossae and they believed in the eternal life prepared for them, this hope moved them to practical love for one another.

entries.section: (2) Praise for their faith and love

paragraphs.text: "You heard and knew": he means knowledge by experience and not theoretical knowledge, a knowledge of the divine gifts and graces and of the heavenly portion as a grace from God.

This Gospel was preached to the people of Colossae, and it also reached the parts of the world that were known at that time, and it bore clear fruit in the lives of those who walk in its commandments throughout the whole world. For the spread of the Gospel the Church prays the litany of the Gospel before the reading of the Gospel in the Divine Liturgy and in her liturgical prayers.

entries.section: (2) Praise for their faith and love

paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul records the fact that the Gospel spread in Colossae through his disciple Epaphras, and he praises him for this and calls him "our dear fellowservant," for servitude to Christ is freedom from sin. He is dear to Paul's heart as a model of the love that binds a father and his son, and he is a faithful servant who labored in the ministry and founded for them their church in Colossae.

entries.section: (2) Praise for their faith and love

paragraphs.text: Epaphras conveyed to St. Paul the virtues and fruits that appeared in the believers of Colossae, which declare a love that is not built on human emotions but is divine love, the fruit of the Holy Spirit working in them.

Look, my brother, to the hope of eternal life, so that your faith may stand firm in the face of afflictions, and hasten to offer love to everyone around you, and you will lay up for yourself a treasure in heaven.

entries.section: (3) A prayer for their spiritual growth

paragraphs.text: Since Epaphras told Paul of the love and faith of the people of Colossae, St. Paul lifts up his heart in prayer for them, that they may be filled with the true knowledge that God wants to teach us, which also guards us from heresies. For the true knowledge of God's will spares us the troubles of falling into the innovations of the philosophers and the heresies of those who claim knowledge. Christian wisdom is the knowledge of the sound Christian principles, so that our conduct in virtue is their practical application.

entries.section: (3) A prayer for their spiritual growth

paragraphs.text: Wisdom and understanding give them the ability to walk spiritually according to the divine commandment, which makes them bear good works that bring them near to God, so that their knowledge of Him increases, and consequently their love for Him.

The children of God have a way of life that differs from that of the children of the world, for they are the light of the world and the salt of the earth. May we make this stand out in our daily conduct in the society in which we live.

entries.section: (3) A prayer for their spiritual growth

paragraphs.text: Spiritual conduct needs spiritual strength. For this reason the Apostle prays for the people of Colossae, that God may grant them strength from Himself according to His infinite power and His unlimited glory, the strength that gives us patience in trials and afflictions and in bearing with others, especially the troublesome among them, with longsuffering. And we rejoice in the midst of afflictions and sufferings because our joy does not depend on outward circumstances but rests on the supporting power of God.
May we be longsuffering, and not murmur or become angry at the sufferings and storms that may meet us, but rejoice, knowing that all things work together for good.

We thank God our Father, who did not leave us to perish when we fell, but gave His only begotten Son to renew our nature and to prepare us to share with the believers in their inheritance, which is the Kingdom of Heaven, after we received in Baptism the sacrament of illumination, so that we now walk as children of light and experience God, the true Light, in our lives.

God the Father delivered us from the power of the devil, so that all the powers of darkness no longer have authority over us, because God bought us with His blood and freed us from the power of Satan. For the victorious Christ, who defeated Satan by the Cross, broke our chains and will lead us in the procession of His triumph to Paradise, which is the Kingdom of Christ. The Kingdom is ascribed to Christ because the Son and the Father are one in essence (Jn 10:30).
God forgave us our sins through the blood of His Son, which was shed on the Cross, and which cleanses us from all our sins and iniquities.

"Image": Christ is the image of God. Its rendering in the Greek is "of the same nature," as when we say that Peter has the image of a man, which means that Peter is a man. The Greek did not use the word that means a mere image of any person or natural scene or anything else drawn on paper, cloth or wood. That is, Paul here affirms that Christ is God.
"The invisible God": because He cannot be perceived by the human senses, but became visible through His Incarnation.

"Firstborn": in the original Greek it is "prototokos," which means the first-born. Indeed Christ the Son is begotten of the Father before all ages, that is, eternal like the Father, as we say in the Creed. "The firstborn of every creature": what is meant is that He is the foremost, who surpasses all creation, that is, the head of every creature, and the beginning of creation and its Maker. The word "firstborn" does not mean priority in existence but denotes priority in greatness and glory.
The Apostle declares that Christ is God, of the same nature, and eternal before all the creation that He created.
"For by him were all things created ...": the Father willed to create, and He created all things by His Word, that is, the Son. Christ, therefore, is the Creator of all.
"That are in heaven": the invisible creatures in heaven, such as all the orders and heavenly powers.
"That are in earth": the visible creatures on earth.
"Whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers": ranks of angels.

"All things were created by him, and for him": one of the important verses in proving the divinity of Christ. Creation came about "by Him," so He is the Creator, and it was created subject "to Him" because He is its Owner and Maker.
Paul shows the divinity of Christ, who created all creatures that are on earth or in heaven, and they are subject to Him and worship Him.
"Before all things": Christ exists before all things, that is, He is eternal; His existence precedes existence.
"By him all things consist": that is, He is the One who laid down the order by which creation proceeds and the laws that preserve the universe and ensure its coherence and harmony.
Christ is eternal before all creatures, and He is their Maker and Ruler, and they live and move by Him.

"The firstborn from the dead": Christ is the only One, and the first, who rose and did not die a second time. Therefore He is the firstborn from the dead, those who will rise in the likeness of His resurrection at the Second Coming. He has gone before us in the resurrection from the dead and we follow Him, and He will go before us in glory in the procession of His triumph.

Christ is the head of the Church, which He bought with His blood, and He does the work of the head with respect to the body. Just as the head leads the body and the body obeys all the signals sent to it from the brain, so Christ leads the Church and gathers the believers to be one, giving them growth and knowledge. It is the duty of the Church to obey Christ completely and for the members to be in complete harmony, so that she takes on the glorious form that Christ, the "Head," desires for her.
"Dwell": in the original Greek it is in the continuous present tense. That is, in Christ the indwelling of the divinity in the humanity is a permanent indwelling.
"Fulness": the divinity in its entirety.
In Christ all the divinity dwelt in the womb of the Virgin Mary, and the divinity never parted from the humanity.
"All": everyone who believed in Christ.

In our fall we were far from God and it was not in our power to return to Him. Therefore the Father reconciled us to Himself by the blood of Christ on the Cross, and this reconciliation of ours with God has given us to be reconciled with all the believers on earth. As for reconciliation with those in heaven, it is the joy of the angels over the salvation of man, for they rejoice over every sinner who repents, or over his being reconciled to God. And since the believers on earth have been reconciled to God, they have consequently been reconciled with the heavenly beings, as we pray in the Liturgy of St. Gregory, saying, "You reconciled the earthly with the heavenly and made the two one." The word "reconcile" in the Greek means the restoring of a lost friend, that is, the friendship of the angels toward us had been lost, and Christ restored it by the salvation that He accomplished for us on the Cross.

The Colossians can verify that reconciliation by the change that has taken place in their lives. They were formerly strangers, not of the commonwealth of God but enemies to Him by their evil thoughts and works, but now, after their reconciliation with God, they walk in the new and pure life.

"The body of his flesh": the union of the divinity with the humanity means God's acceptance of mankind. Christ in His body is the representative of mankind; that is, the Incarnation is the beginning of the reconciliation, which is then completed by redemption and the Resurrection. "Unblameable": God will not condemn you for a sin, because Christ has justified you since you believed and repented. "Unreproveable": the accusation of the devil against the children of God.

Christ accepted death in order to slay the enmity and to raise you from the death of sin by His glorious Resurrection, so that you may live a new life after He has purified you and washed you from your sins, to bring you on the last day to the Father in your new form, the form of holiness and righteousness without blemish, and so you deprive the accuser, that is, Satan, of the opportunity to stand and protest before God against you.

You share in the responsibility for the salvation of your souls, by continuing in the faith and not being moved, and by holding fast to the Gospel that you heard from the faithful servant Epaphras, which has been preached to every creature, the Gospel for whose spread among the Gentiles I have labored and striven, that I might win them to Christ.

May we live in holiness so that we may have a share in the procession of triumph, and so that we do not merely reject evil, which is the negative side of striving, but do what is right and good and strive to acquire the virtues.

St. Paul rejoices in the sufferings of ministry because they are a fellowship in the sufferings of Christ's crucifixion. The atoning sufferings of Christ are complete, but He gives us the opportunity to share His sufferings in serving souls and winning them to Him. These are the hardships and labors of ministry, and they are "lacking" because many souls are still far away and need us to serve them and bring them to Him, so that we fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ. That is, every labor in ministry is a fellowship in the sufferings of Christ, which we fill up in our bodies, that is, by the weariness of the body for the growth of the Church, the body of Christ.
"For its sake": that is, for the Church.
God chose me and set me apart for your service, O Gentiles, according to His saving plan for you, that I might fulfil the preaching in His holy name.

The preaching of salvation to the Gentiles is the hidden mystery that the Jews did not understand, because they considered themselves alone to be those who would obtain the salvation of Christ, and the Gentiles did not know it because they were immersed in idolatry and lusts. But in the New Testament this mystery was revealed through the faith of the Gentiles, and the believers from among the Gentiles, that is, the saints, enjoyed the salvation of Christ.
God made known to the Gentiles who believed in Him His abundant blessings, which they receive through their faith in Christ, not only in the Church but also in the eternal inheritance.

This is the One whom we proclaim to all, warning every man who sins and offering him the profitable teaching, marked by the wisdom of the Spirit working in us, about the truths of the Christian faith, so that he may reject the teachings of the false teachers; and this with the aim of bringing every man to God step by step on the way of perfection, which is accomplished only by union with Christ. For the sake of this aim I labor and strive, moved by the Lord's mighty working in me, for it is He who gives me the understanding, the ability and the zeal to achieve my salvation and the salvation of others.

You are responsible for showing Christ to everyone by your love, and for teaching everyone who sins so that he may repent, but with wisdom, love and humility, so that you gladden the heart of God and make glad all who are distressed.
The salvation of Christ and keeping away from false teachings
"What great conflict": its Greek origin expresses excessive concern and intense striving.

Paul wanted to affirm his fatherhood and his concern for the people of Colossae and the people of Laodicea, the large city neighboring it, lest they think that he did not care for them because he had not gone to them and seen them.
"Riches": generosity and abundance.
"Full assurance of understanding": complete comprehension.
"The mystery of God, and of the Father": the depths of the unlimited essence of God.

"And of Christ": the Incarnation of Christ showed us God: "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (Jn 1:18). Paul's striving in Colossae and Laodicea had three aims:
The first: the comforting of their hearts by the Holy Spirit dwelling in them, so that they may be strengthened and encouraged in facing difficult situations.
The second: that their hearts may be knit together and bound with the bond of perfect love.
The third: that they may be filled with complete understanding, so that they may know the mystery of God the Father dwelling in Christ, which has become revealed to all in Christ.

All the treasures of wisdom, knowledge and understanding are hidden from eternity in the hypostasis of the Word, our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Apostle called them treasures because they are of great benefit to whoever grasps them.
"Enticing words": that is, flattery.

"I say this": that is, his words about Christ contain all that is sufficient for our salvation and also our spiritual satisfaction, so we have no need to know any other philosophy. And I say this lest anyone deceive you with words that adorn falsehood and clothe it in the garments of truth, that is, words whose outside attracts those who hear them while their inside carries deadly poison, and these are the words of the false teachers.

May we not be deceived by the errors that some people promote in these days and wrap in sweet, smooth talk with which they hunt innocent victims. We who walk in the truth have no need of this flattery, but we receive true knowledge from our mother the Church, rich in the sayings of the Fathers who handed down to us the right faith. So do not allow anyone to enter your house and interpret the Holy Bible to you unless you are sure that he is a responsible servant sent by the fathers of the Church.

Paul declares that although he had not visited Colossae and Laodicea, he is occupied with them and with their circumstances and their striving in prayers for him, and he follows their news as if he were living with them in heart and spirit, and he rejoices when he sees their keeping of order in the Church. Their holding fast to the rite of the Church and their strong faith repel the erroneous ideas that intrude, and so they form a solid front that the enemies of the Church cannot penetrate.
As you received Christ in the simplicity of faith as your Savior and Redeemer, walk also in His commandments so that you may acquire a life of holiness.

The Apostle Paul calls them to stand firm in the faith as Epaphras preached it to them, like a tree that is rooted by its roots and a building whose foundation is deep. Then he shows their distinction from one another in their care for thanking God.

Beware and be careful lest anyone gain mastery over your minds, so that vain philosophy and false teachings, which people proclaim and which agree with human material ideas, draw you away; consequently their source is not Christ and they do not agree with His teachings.
The divinity dwells in Christ in His humanity with a permanent indwelling.

"The fulness of the Godhead": a word that the Greek philosophers and the Gnostics used to express the essence and the divine exaltedness. There was a theory of the fulness which claimed that there must be a chain of intermediaries between this fulness and human beings, and that Christ is the last of these intermediaries. This led St. Paul to affirm that Christ is not an intermediary but is the fulness itself, since in Him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily, that is, He alone is God. This verse is a clear proof of the divinity of Christ.

You who believe in Him are filled by Him with the spiritual gifts and blessings that you need for your salvation. The Lord Christ is the head of all the heavenly orders and all human authorities, for He is the One who created them, and He is also the head of the Church because He is her founder and redeemer.
"The putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh": the death of the old man, which is the nature inclined to evil, from which we are freed by Baptism.

Among the claims of the Judaizers was the necessity of circumcision of the flesh, and St. Paul answers them, explaining that spiritual circumcision, that is, circumcision of the heart, which is the cutting off of the nature inclined to evil and living a new life with God, this is the circumcision of Christ that He gives us in the Church in the sacrament of Baptism.

You have been renewed through fellowship with Christ in His death and Resurrection, for you were buried with Him in Baptism, where your sins were buried. Baptism is not only a tomb for us, but a tomb and a resurrection, so we rise with the new nature to walk in the new life with Christian conduct, by the power of the faith that we have in the power of God.
"The uncircumcision of your flesh": the lack of circumcision of the flesh, accompanied by the evil inclinations within the unbeliever.

You Colossians were formerly Gentiles under the rule of spiritual death because of your sins and your evil inclinations that governed your conduct, but God raised you from your eternal death with the Resurrection of His Son Jesus Christ, and freed you from the slavery of sin by the death of His Son, who bore for you all the weight of sin on the Cross and forgave you all your sins.

Because of the nature of man, which became corrupt after the Fall, he was unable to obey the Law, so that all came under the rule of death. But Christ, to whom be glory, when He died on the Cross, fulfilled by His death all the debts that were upon mankind, and God took away the handwriting that was against us, that is, the document in which all our disobedience to the commandments of the Law was recorded, so that the Law no longer had any claim against us, for that document was nailed to the Cross of Christ. This is an expression taken from the ancient custom in Roman society, when a law was abolished: they would lift it up to fix it with a nail on something high.
"Principalities and powers": the ranks of the fallen angels, that is, the demons.

By the death of Christ on the Cross, God stripped Satan and all his evil forces of their authority over us, exposing the shame of the powers of evil before all, so that they became like captives before the procession of the victorious Christ.

If Christ has renewed our nature and forgiven our sins in the sacrament of Baptism, we ought to live as His children and use our new nature in spiritual aspirations so that we may enjoy fellowship with Him in prayers, readings, meditations and service by which we show our love for Him, and so grow every day in the knowledge of Him.

The Law in the Old Testament forbade eating some foods as a training for beginners in distinguishing between what is right and what is wrong. Likewise the Law of the Old Testament commanded the observance of certain occasions, such as feasts, the new moon or the Sabbath day, as days of rest. But St. Paul forbids them to let anyone judge them by the Jewish ordinances, because the purpose of all these has been fulfilled by the coming of Christ, so these ordinances no longer have any meaning, for Christ Jesus is our true rest. But in the New Testament this verse does not conflict with attention to the fasts and feasts, because fasting has a new meaning in the Church, which is being occupied away from material things by the love of Christ, and the feasts are a remembrance of the salvation of Christ.
"Which are a shadow": the works of the Law.

"Things to come": what had to be accomplished, that is, the new life in the Church of the New Testament. "The body": the body of Christ, that is, the Church in which all the types have been fulfilled.

All these things were shadows of what was fulfilled in the New Testament by the Incarnation of Christ, His redemption of us and the appearance of the Church of the New Testament, which is the body of Christ; with her appearing the shadows disappeared and no longer have any importance. For when that which is signified comes, the type is made void.

"Worshipping of angels": the Gnostics proclaimed that God is too exalted to create the world, so He created spiritual beings, that is, angels, the last of whom was Christ, and by him the world was created. So they proclaimed the worship of Christ as one of the angels, and of all these degrees of angels. This is of course a teaching foreign to Christianity, which believes that Christ is God and created the material world Himself, because matter is sacred in Him.

St. Paul warns them lest they lose the reward that has been prepared for them, that is, eternal life, by listening to false teachers who think that by calling for the worship of angels they show humility in order to gain the praise of people. It is a false humility and a sin clothed in the garments of virtue. These persons falsely claimed that they had seen angels, while what they claimed as visions was no more than the product of their minds, which have the fleshly rational thinking that leads to pride, and not the thinking that is subject to the powers of the Spirit.

This thinking is thinking separated from the Head, that is, Christ, and does not live according to Him. Christ is the head of the Church, who gathers all in His body by a spiritual bond, so that the body is knit together, expressing complete unity of thought, achieving for it spiritual growth in holiness from God.
If you, by your death with Christ, have risen with a new nature, why do you live according to the principles of the world?

You are now living in the age of grace and have become free from the rule of the Law, so do not walk in the ordinances and teachings of men, which have no value, those things which the Law imposed and the false teachers added to, forbidding other additional things such as not touching or eating certain foods (Lev 21:1, 5:2, 3).

These are things that are consumed and pass away, and urging adherence to them is no more than human teaching according to the whims of the false teachers, who go to excess in holding to the formalities of the old worship.
"Will worship": worship in excess of what God has appointed.

The commandments and traditions of men have the appearance and form of wisdom while they are in truth entirely far from true wisdom. They are a formal worship that is not now required and profits nothing, and a humility that is rejected because it is outward, and a humiliation of the body, which these false teachers regard as a source of evil. All these things are of no value and do not satisfy the human soul, which nothing truly satisfies but attachment to God.

May you be aware of every act of worship you offer to God, so that you understand the words of the prayer and turn what you read in the Holy Bible into practical application, and your holding fast to the rites of the Church may be with awareness, so that the rite stirs your feelings toward God.
The attributes of the children of God

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: Since you have risen with Christ, you must seek what befits your new nature, so direct your concern toward heavenly things and the things that qualify you for the eternal inheritance, and place your hope in the heavenly Kingdom, where Christ sits in the highest place.

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: Occupy your thoughts with the heavenly Kingdom and care for it and for everything that qualifies you for it, and do not care for the world and material things and everything that would bind you to the earth.

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: For when you were baptized you were buried with Christ, and so you died to sin and were freed from its dominion, and thereby you cut all the ties that bound you to the world.

The Greeks used to say of the dead person that he is hidden or concealed in the earth, and St. Paul uses the same expression, saying that after we died with Christ our life became hidden or concealed in Him. And just as the Gnostics claimed that the knowledge necessary for salvation is hidden in their books and concealed from the eyes of the world, we know that our life is hidden in Christ, our salvation and our hope, and concealed from the eyes of the world, who do not understand and do not want to understand the mystery of salvation.

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: "Shall appear": God will make Him appear at His Second Coming.
We now live in Christ, so when He comes in His glory at His Second Coming, we too will be glorified with Him.

Remember that you rose with Christ when you came up out of the water of Baptism and when you partake of His life-giving Body and Blood. So reject every sin into which you fall, because it is foreign to you, and seek in its place a life with God in prayers that lift you up to heaven.

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: The Apostle asks them to put to death the fleshly lusts that are committed by the members of the body, and here he lists five sins, which are:

"Fornication": which is the breaking of one of the Ten Commandments, "Thou shalt not commit adultery." There is also the figurative meaning of fornication, which is spiritual fornication, namely forsaking God and worshiping strange gods, as ancient paganism did in former times, and what is equivalent to it in the present times, the worship of money, position, fame ... etc.
"Uncleanness": which is the natural fruit of fornication and of sin in general, for sin defiles the heart, the mind, the body and the spirit.
"Inordinate affection": that is, unholy emotions, abnormal desires and the pursuit of pleasure.
"Evil concupiscence": a material desire against the commandments of God.

"Covetousness": the increasing desire to possess. Covetousness has been described as idolatry because it is attachment to material things, and if a person persists in it, he places all his hopes in them and offers them worship. By covetousness St. Paul may here mean covetousness in sexual matters, since he mentions it in connection with the sins of the flesh, such as a person coveting and lusting after a woman who is not lawful for him, whether another man's wife or any girl.

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: Because of these sins the wrath of God comes upon those who commit them, and the Apostle called them "children of disobedience" since they hold fast to disobedience to the end and so are ascribed to it. In addition, the sins of the flesh sometimes carry their punishment in themselves, such as the diseases associated with uncleanness, the latest of which is AIDS.

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: You Colossians were formerly among those who commit those sins, for the pagan Gentiles considered uncleanness a part of the rites of their worship, and you lived in an evil environment and so you walked according to its evil beliefs.

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: But now be freed from those vices and walk in the Spirit, and cast your former bitter sins far from you so that they do not cast you into outer darkness; the iniquities of the past and what has come from you are enough. St. Paul here points to five other sins, which are:
"Anger": which is the result of hatred, malice, and the loss of love and forbearance.
"Wrath": a violent expression of dissatisfaction with a certain attitude coming from others.
"Malice": the evil that holds within it the desire to harm others and to blame them.
"Blasphemy": cursing and slandering God, and its punishment in the Old Testament was death. "Filthy communication": improper words and silly sexual jokes.

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: St. Paul forbids lying, which is not telling the truth out of many motives, such as trying to obtain some undeserved advantages, or fear, or a sense of inferiority, or joking, and it brings a chain of dependent sins such as false swearing and then anger. It is not right for us to deceive others and lie to them, when what is right is that we must tell them the truth and not lies. So he calls them to leave the works that were characteristic of the fallen nature of man before renewal, especially since they have received the new nature, which grows and is renewed in the knowledge of God through spiritual striving until it becomes a true image of Him.

entries.section: (1) Concern for heavenly things and abandoning sin

paragraphs.text: In this new nature you all become one in Christ, for the Lord Christ broke down the barriers between the Jews and the Gentiles. St. Paul mentioned certain classifications of people, namely: "Greek": who had a distinguished standing in society from the founding of the Greek Empire and even after the domination of the Roman Empire, and the Roman looked on one who did not speak Greek as a backward barbarian.
"Jew": one who prided himself on being a son of Abraham and had the Law and the promises, and the rest of the peoples were in his view unclean dogs.
"Circumcision": the Jews who are circumcised in their bodies in application of the Law.
"Uncircumcision": the peoples other than the Jews, who are not circumcised.
"Barbarian": one who does not speak Greek, who was looked upon with contempt.
"Scythian": one who lives north of the Black Sea; they were the harshest and most savage of the barbarians, so that the mere mention of their name stirred terror in souls.
"Bondman": one who had no human rights, and whose master had absolute freedom over him.

All of these, despite the great differences among them, if they accepted the faith, all became members of the one body of Christ, so that the whole body became the body of Christ, just as Christ dwelt in the hearts of all and so united them.
"Bowels of mercies": gentleness toward others springing from feelings of deep love.
"Meekness": the inward calm of the heart.

You Colossians, as those chosen by the Lord who loved you and redeemed you, adorn yourselves with the attributes and virtues of Christ and follow His example in compassion, humility, meekness and longsuffering.

Just as God bore with us and forgave us, and still does, so we must forgive our brethren if they wrong us. What helps us in this is our being adorned with the virtues mentioned in the previous verse. And our forgiveness of others is because God freely forgives us all our sins.
Above all the virtues mentioned, adorn yourselves with love, for it is the garment that gathers within it all the other virtues.
Hold fast to the peace that you obtained in the one body of Christ, and keep away from everything that disturbs your hearts, and give thanks to God for all His gifts.

Let the teachings of Christ dwell in you and abide in your hearts with a permanent abiding, and you must know them, so that you acquire all divine wisdom for dealing with others and for winning souls for the Kingdom by teaching them the foundation of the spiritual life and warning them to keep away from sin, using the Psalms, with their prayers of thanksgiving and praise that lift the soul to heaven, and the spiritual songs that stir in the soul reverence and spiritual joy, taking care for depth and spirituality so that your hearts touch the divine grace.
"In the name of the Lord Jesus": with the aim of pleasing Christ and for the glory of His blessed name. "By him": by Christ, by whose help and salvation we draw near to God and give Him thanks.
Let Christ be the aim of all your works and words, and give thanks to God for the salvation and the divine help.

Love is what moves every Christian, so look at God's love for you so that you give Him thanks and return love for love, and so overflow with mercy, tenderness and sacrifice for all who are around you.

entries.section: (3) Advice to the members of the Christian family

paragraphs.text: The Apostle advises wives to submit to their husbands as they submit to the Lord. The wife offers submission to her husband as a sacrifice of love to Christ first, before it is to please her husband, and this suits the nature of the man, whose first demand is respect and appreciation, which moves him to meet the first demand of the woman, which is love, self-giving and kind words. Submission does not mean the man's domination but his leadership of the family, while decisions, after this submission, are made through understanding and love.

entries.section: (3) Advice to the members of the Christian family

paragraphs.text: He also instructs men to love their wives as Christ loved the Church, for the bond between them is like the bond between Christ and the Church. Just as Christ gave Himself on the Cross for the Church, offering the highest feelings of love, so the husband must care for his wife and express his love for her every day with words of praise and support her in every need, and not use his leadership or his means to dominate her or be harsh toward her.

entries.section: (3) Advice to the members of the Christian family

paragraphs.text: Children must obey their parents in all things, and the only condition for obeying parents is that it not conflict with the commandments of the Lord.

entries.section: (3) Advice to the members of the Christian family

paragraphs.text: St. Paul advises fathers not to be severe in dealing with their children and not to increase their rebuking and punishing of them, lest they lose confidence in themselves and their personalities be shaken. They should not be asked for more than they are able, which helps them to carry out the commandment of obedience, so that he is pleased with them.

For your family to be truly Christian, you must feel the presence of Christ with you inside your home. Then you will care for the other party for the sake of Christ, who sees and hears everything you do and say. And you will care for your children with longsuffering, embracing them as Christ embraces your family.
"Your masters according to the flesh": that is, the earthly masters, because the spiritual Master, that is, God, is the most important, so we work to please Him in our dealings with our superiors.
"Eyeservice": pleasing the eyes of the masters while the heart is troubled by them or tries to neglect their orders. "Singleness of heart": purity and humility.

The Apostle instructs slaves to obey their masters who own them according to the laws by which society then operated. And he instructs them to be faithful in service, not in order that their masters may praise them but out of fear of the Lord.

Slaves must do the work required of them as if the work they do is offered to the Lord, doing it with sincerity and faithfulness of heart, knowing that the Lord will reward them for their faithfulness by making them sharers in the inheritance of eternal glory.
Those who treat others unjustly and are harsh to them, exploiting their authority in doing so, these will receive just retribution from God, who shows no partiality to anyone.

The fear of God protects you from many sins, and if you fall it makes you hasten to repentance and reassures your heart whatever the threats of others, and it moves you to love everyone, so that you receive divine tenderness and love. The Christian and society, then the conclusion

entries.section: (1) Dealing with society and serving it

paragraphs.text: The Apostle asks the masters who own slaves to be gentle with them and not to wrong them, knowing that they are human beings like themselves, warning them that there is a higher Master for all, who is God, who judges for the wronged and takes vengeance on those who wrong them.

entries.section: (1) Dealing with society and serving it

paragraphs.text: St. Paul gives the people of Colossae further spiritual advice, asking them to persevere in prayer, for it is the commandment of the Lord Christ to us (Lk 18:1), so we do not cease from prayer for any reason. Prayer must be with vigor and attention, giving thanks to God always, expressing our submission to the divine will and handing over all our affairs to Him.

entries.section: (1) Dealing with society and serving it

paragraphs.text: At the beginning of his epistle Paul told them that he prays for them at all times, and at the end of the epistle here he asks for their prayers for him, that God may open before him the closed doors in preaching, remove the obstacles from the path of ministry, prepare minds to hear the word of God, and open hearts to faith when he speaks of the mystery of Christ, that is, the salvation that Christ accomplished for all and the opening of the door of faith to the Gentiles, for the preaching of which he was imprisoned.

entries.section: (1) Dealing with society and serving it

paragraphs.text: "Them that are without": that is, the unbelievers.

"Redeeming the time": seizing the opportunity to work so that it is not wasted on what profits nothing. God instructs us to be wise as serpents (Mt 10:16). Wisdom requires walking uprightly, carefully and blamelessly, especially in our dealings with unbelievers, so that our mixing with them is within limits, for they watch our conduct, on the basis of which they glorify our Father who is in heaven or blaspheme Him because of us.

entries.section: (1) Dealing with society and serving it

paragraphs.text: When grace dwells in our hearts, our speech is with love, gentleness and humility, and so it imparts grace to the hearers. Just as salt is put in food so that the one who eats may taste it, so let your speech be marked by meekness and gentleness so that it may be easily accepted by others.

Seek God before every word or action, and He will guide you by His wisdom to all that is good, and will cover your weakness and even glorify you in the eyes of others, so that they see in you the love of God and His righteousness and love Him because of you.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: In this passage St. Paul sends them the greetings of ten of his disciples who work with him in the Lord's vineyard, namely:
Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus who is called Justus, Epaphras, Luke, Demas, Nymphas, Archippus.

He begins by praising Tychicus and calls him a beloved brother, raising him to be on an equal footing with himself, although he is his disciple, giving us a lesson in humility. Tychicus was a faithful servant who carried out his ministry with diligence and perseverance. He will make known to the people of Colossae the news of Paul so that they may be reassured about him.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: St. Paul also sent his disciple Tychicus to Colossae to learn their news and to encourage them in the spiritual life.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: Paul sent with Tychicus another disciple, Onesimus, who is a slave of Philemon, who lived in the city of Colossae, which is why Paul says of him, "who is one of you." He will undertake with Tychicus to inform the people of Colossae of what is happening in Rome, where St. Paul is imprisoned.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: He conveys to them the greeting of Aristarchus, who is imprisoned with him, and also the greeting of St. Mark, the nephew of Barnabas and Paul's companion on many journeys. St. Paul had earlier sent recommendations on his behalf to the churches of Asia Minor, so that they would receive him as an apostle of Christ, and he repeats this recommendation here.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: "Jesus, which is called Justus": one of Paul's disciples, who also sends his greeting to the people of Colossae.
"Who are of the circumcision": he means Aristarchus, Mark and Justus, because they are of Jewish origin and circumcised as the Law requires.
"Only": the disciples of Paul mentioned here are the ones who were helping him in preaching at that time in Rome.

"Have been a comfort unto me": their sharing with Paul in the ministry comforted and strengthened him in the midst of the affliction of prison. This shows the humility of Paul, who declares his need for comfort and encouragement from his children. Those whom Paul mentioned work with him to spread the word of the Gospel, and they became a comfort to him in the time of affliction.

Be strong and face yourself to know your spiritual, psychological and material needs, so that you ask for them from God and thank everyone who provides them to you, however much younger or lesser than you he may be, for this teaches you humility and encourages and gladdens the others whom you thank.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: He sends them the greetings of Epaphras, who is from among the Gentiles, a disciple of Paul and the founder of the three churches of Phrygia (Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis), and he called him a servant of Christ, for he is one of the heroes of the faith. Epaphras was a beautiful example of perseverance in prayer, and he strove in it so that the Lord might grant grace to the believers, that they might stand firm in the faith and not be affected by innovations and heresies, doing the will of God.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: St. Paul noticed the fervent prayer of Epaphras, so he bore witness to his zeal for the salvation of his children in the faith and his care for them and for the churches he founded in Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: He sends them the greeting of Luke the physician, who combined the two virtues of love and mercy, which he acquired from his original profession as a physician. Before his faith he treated only bodies, but after his faith he became a physician of souls and bodies.

"Demas": the only one of the ten disciples who did not receive a single word of praise from his teacher Paul, perhaps because he sensed the inclination of his heart toward the present world. And this indeed happened, and it is mentioned in (2 Tim 4:10) where he said of him, "Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world."

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: Paul sends his greeting to the brethren in Laodicea, which is very near to Colossae, since with it and the neighboring city of Hierapolis it forms the region of preaching of Epaphras, the disciple of Paul.
"Nymphas": one of the well-to-do Laodicean brethren, who opened his house as a church for the worship of the believers.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: Here Paul asks the people of Colossae to send this epistle after reading it to Laodicea to be read there, and that they ask Laodicea for the epistle that Paul had sent to them so that it may be read among them also. The commentators agree that the epistle meant is the Epistle to the Ephesians, because it was addressed to all the churches neighboring Ephesus and not only to the church of Ephesus.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: "Archippus": a servant in the church of Colossae, perhaps an assistant to Epaphras, who led the church during his absence in Rome when he visited Paul. Some think that he was the son of Philemon because he is mentioned in the epistle sent to him.

Paul's charge to Archippus is directed to every servant, and it is that the ministry he carries out is in Christ, so he should care for it and complete it by the power of God and for His sake, so that a servant does not begin a ministry and then become negligent in it or in any of its details.

entries.section: (2) Greetings from Paul and his disciples

paragraphs.text: The heretics used to forge the epistles of St. Paul, so he would put a mark on his epistle by writing this last phrase in addition to his signature on the epistle.

"Remember my bonds": the Apostle gives them an example of faithfulness and self-giving sacrifice, so that they do not weaken before persecutions, but remember the labors of their teacher, so that their souls are filled with readiness for self-giving and sacrifice in his likeness. St. Paul ends his epistle by asking grace for them, which suffices them and enriches them.
Paul wrote this epistle from within his prison in Rome, and he dictated it to his two disciples Tychicus and Onesimus.
